scale: Each criterion is scored 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5 or 2 against written anchors. Case score = 5 x weighted average, 0 to 10. The weights and the four steps are a design, not fitted to data.

criteria.name: Outcomes with numbers
criteria.question: What changed in the last 12 months because of you? For each: the number before, the number after, and who outside your team noticed.

levels.0: Projects, tasks, activity. "I worked on", "I was responsible for". Or a problem with no result yet.
levels.1: At least one outcome with a before and an after number, or a change the business names without you (a report that stopped, a complaint that ended).
levels.2: Three or more outcomes, each with a number and what the business got from it (money, time, risk, customers). People outside the team name them without you in the room.

moves.month: Pick your two biggest pieces of work and find the before and after number for each. Ask the PM or finance for the business side.
moves.quarter: Agree one measurable outcome with your manager now, so the next review writes itself.

criteria.name: The next level, already done
criteria.question: Which of the next level's signals (see tracks) can you show today, with a date and a person who saw it?

levels.0: Fewer than two signals of the next level have evidence. The case rests on doing the current job well.
levels.1: About half of the next level's signals have evidence, each with an example and a date.
levels.2: All signals but at most one have evidence, kept up for months, and at least one was seen by someone above your manager.

moves.month: Take the next level's missing signal that is cheapest to show and do it once, where your manager can see it.
moves.quarter: Turn that signal into a habit: three times in a quarter, not once.

criteria.name: Scope and its growth
criteria.question: What did you own when you got your current title, and what do you own now? People, systems, teams, budget, decisions.

levels.0: The same scope as when you got the current title.
levels.1: Scope grew, and you can say what was added and when.
levels.2: For six months or more you have carried most of the next level's scope, and the people around you treat it as yours.

moves.month: Write your scope twice: when you got the title and today. Show it to your manager and ask if it matches theirs.
moves.quarter: Ask for one piece of the next level's scope that nobody owns today.

criteria.name: Decisions and proposals
criteria.question: Which open decision did you close, and which proposal did you bring that nobody asked for?

levels.0: You deliver what was agreed. No decision closed or proposal made by you.
levels.1: One decision unblocked or one proposal made in the last six months: options, a recommended default, a date.
levels.2: Several, including one proposal nobody asked for (a number, a problem, a bet), each written down with what was decided and who owns it.

moves.month: Find the decision your team has left open for weeks. Write a one-pager: three options, your default, a date. Get the two people who disagree into one room.
moves.quarter: Bring one proposal nobody asked for to a leadership meeting: a number, a problem, a bet.

criteria.name: People who vouch
criteria.question: Who would tell the decider, unprompted, what you did? What did each of them see?

levels.0: Nobody named, or only "people like working with me".
levels.1: One or two named people who saw specific work, wherever they sit.
levels.2: Three or more named people, at least one outside your team or one level above your manager, who saw specific work and know you are going for the next level.

moves.month: Name three people who saw your best work. Tell each of them what you are going for and ask what they saw.
moves.quarter: Do one piece of work with a leader outside your team, so a second voice exists.

criteria.name: Your manager has a stake
criteria.question: Does your manager know what you are going for, and what did they say they need to see, by when?

levels.0: Your manager does not know you want the next level.
levels.0.5: Your manager heard a general interest once ("I'm interested in management"), without the target level or a date.
levels.1: Your manager knows the target level and roughly when, but you have not agreed what they need to see.
levels.2: You asked "what would you need to see from me by <date>?", got a short list, and check progress against it in your 1:1s.

moves.month: In your next 1:1: "I want to go for <level>. What would you need to see from me by <month>?" Write the answer down and send it back to them.
moves.quarter: Check the list once a month in your 1:1. No surprises at review time.

steps.name: Quiet work
steps.line: The work may well be real. The case cannot see it yet.

steps.name: On the runway
steps.line: The evidence is building. Agree the criteria and the date, then keep going.

steps.name: Almost there
steps.line: Close the top gap, then ask.

steps.name: Ready to ask
steps.line: Ask, show the evidence, then stop talking.

gate: If 'manager' is below 1, the step is capped at 3 (Almost there): a manager who hears about it for the first time at the promotion conversation has no evidence and no stake. The first conversation is the early ask, not the promotion ask.

to_mid.name: Junior to mid-level engineer
signals: Breaks big problems into small, valuable increments
Asks product the why behind what ships
Helps people in other teams
Owns a piece of functionality from idea to production to the customer
to_mid.trap: Lack of workflow ownership: you have built parts, never carried one piece end to end.

to_senior.name: Mid-level to senior engineer
signals: Multiplier effect: was the buddy of a new starter, or helped someone reach their delivery goals
Brings thought-through proposals on their own
Pairs and shares knowledge instead of taking the exciting feature alone
Proof of a process improvement the team still uses
Asked for a learning budget (course, conference) in the last 12 months and shared what came back
to_senior.trap: Impressive alone. Being strong solo does not make you senior; the multiplier effect does.

to_staff.name: Senior to staff or principal engineer
signals: Communicates well enough that people outside engineering follow the technical argument
Owns and executes part of the technical roadmap
Leads an internal community of practice and keeps it active
Speaks in public (meetup, podcast, conference) at least twice a year
Colleagues from other teams seek their input
to_staff.trap: Working solo in the corner: the multiplier effect is missing.

to_lead.name: Senior engineer or tech lead to team lead or engineering manager
signals: Closed an epic that was slipping: took it over, cut what would not be missed, finished it
Delivered value the business names without you in the room
Closed a decision that had been open for weeks: one-pager, three options, a default, a date, owners written down
Has done the people part already (1:1s, feedback, onboarding) and prefers it over coding
to_lead.trap: Internal refactors offered as the main evidence. Good engineering, weak evidence. And the stay-IC signal: if you prefer coding over taking care of people, say so before building the case.

to_director.name: Engineering manager to senior EM, director or VP
signals: Argued a position that cost your own team something and helped the department, out loud
Brought a proposal that was not on the agenda or the roadmap: a number, a problem, a bet
Acted on a piece of hard feedback where people could see it
Leaders above you have seen you argue for the whole department, not only your team
to_director.trap: Flawless execution of someone else's roadmap. The EM who executes perfectly is invisible at promotion time.
self_test: Did I argue any position that cost my team something?
Did I bring anything that wasn't already on the agenda or the roadmap?
What did I do with the last piece of hard feedback I received, and who saw me do it?
new_seat: Listen to the strategy end to end, with your manager and the people above
Propose the KPIs yourself and write your own definition of success
Agree the resources those KPIs need, in the same room
Get the mandate over your territory said out loud
